title: Why you snap before you think

scenes.visual: Big navy hook text pops word by word; Norb peeks curious from below.
scenes.cardText: Why do you snap before you can stop yourself?
scenes.voiceover: Why do you snap before you can stop yourself?

scenes.visual: Amygdala character center-stage; red alarm rings fire outward; a mustard threat spark zaps in from the right. Norb watches, panicked.
scenes.voiceover: Deep in your brain sits a smoke detector called the amygdala. The second it senses a threat, it fires an alarm — before you have had a single thought.

scenes.visual: Two race tracks: short coral FAST lane races to a BODY endpoint first; long teal SLOW lane is still mid-way to THINK. Norb jittery.
scenes.voiceover: That alarm takes a shortcut — straight to your body. The thinking part of your brain gets the message later. So you snap first, and reason shows up late.

scenes.visual: A coral urge wave swells high then crashes flat; a small navy anchor stands still, unbothered. Norb gets the idea.
scenes.voiceover: The good news: that surge crests and fades in about ninety seconds — if you don't keep feeding it. Ride the wave instead of acting on it.

scenes.visual: THE SCIENCE card; below it red alarm rings, then an ANGRY label tag spring-drops onto them — rings shrink, calm teal ring blooms. Norb curious.
scenes.cardText:
Name the feeling.
The amygdala quiets when you label the emotion.
scenes.voiceover: Brain scans show that naming a feeling — just saying 'I'm angry' — turns the amygdala's volume down. Researchers call it affect labeling.

scenes.visual: TRY THIS card; below it the wave crests and subsides while a mustard label floats calmly. Norb celebrates.
scenes.cardText:
Name it out loud.
Then give it ninety seconds.
scenes.voiceover: Next time you feel the spike: name it out loud. Then give it ninety seconds before you respond. That's the whole trick.
